pr.title: coverage: Hoist some complex code out of the main span refinement loop
pr.description:
The span refinement loop in `spans.rs` takes the spans that have been extracted from MIR, and modifies them to produce more helpful output in coverage reports.

It is also one of the most complicated pieces of code in the coverage instrumentor. It has an abundance of moving pieces that make it difficult to understand, and most attempts to modify it end up accidentally changing its behaviour in unacceptable ways.

This PR nevertheless tries to make a dent in it by hoisting two pieces of special-case logic out of the main loop, and into separate preprocessing passes. Coverage tests show that the resulting mappings are *almost* identical, with all known differences being unimportant.

This should hopefully unlock further simplifications to the refinement loop, since it now has fewer edge cases to worry about.
pr.author: Zalathar

processing.reason: PR #119208 is a coverage-instrumentation refactor, not a runtime-semantics change. At the PR head (compiler/rustc_mir_transform/src/coverage/spans/from_mir.rs), the hoist explicitly preserves the required order: initial spans are sorted with `cmp_in_dominator_order`, then `remove_unwanted_macro_spans` runs, then `split_visible_macro_spans` appends split spans, and the final span sort runs afterward. The only observable differences are in generated coverage metadata (`.coverage` line counts and `.cov-map` mappings/expressions), e.g. the `debug_assert!` line in tests/coverage/inline-dead.rs becoming covered and closure mapping expression counts changing. Those values are not observable by executing the compiled Rust functions under Miri. Constructing a Rust function pair that models a “dedup before dominator sort” or “split without re-sorting” variant would encode a hypothetical wrong hoist, not the historical merged transformation, and any resulting value difference would come from that fabricated model rather than from a source-grounded runtime regression. Therefore no valid original/transformed function pair with identical signatures and concrete runtime inputs can be validated for this PR.

analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historical transformation is the inline per-refinement-iteration handling above: it only discarded a same-span macro `curr` when it was adjacent to `prev` in the refinement loop, and it split visible macro names relative to `curr_original_span` after merges/cutoffs. Hoisting that behavior into preprocessing is only correct if the preprocessing order is preserved: sort by BCB dominator order, remove unwanted macro spans retaining the first per span, split visible macro spans into name+`!` and remainder, then sort again. A wrong hoist would deduplicate before dominator ordering, or split appended spans without re-sorting, thereby retaining a different macro span or emitting different mappings. The merged patch accepts that old and new mappings are not perfectly identical; test expectations show changed mappings for closure macro spans and for `debug_assert!` in `inline-dead`.
analysis.inputDomain: Rust source functions compiled with coverage instrumentation where branch-expanding macros produce multiple BBs with the same macro-invocation span, where visible macro invocations occur inside or around closures, where the function is async, and where the body may be unreachable or yield no spans. The observable domain is `tests/coverage` output: `.coverage` line-count reports and `.cov-map` raw mapping/expression data, not ordinary runtime behavior.
analysis.originalLogic: The original main refinement loop in `CoverageSpansGenerator` handled macro cases inline. When `prev_original_span == curr.span`, it checked both `prev.visible_macro` and `curr.visible_macro`; if both were macro expansions it called `self.take_curr(); // Discards curr.` for same-span macro-generated BBs, otherwise `update_pending_dups()`. It also called `maybe_push_macro_name_span()` at several loop branch points (initial span, same-BCB merge, non-overlap push, overlap cutoff), splitting `curr` at `self.curr_original_span.lo() + BytePos(visible_macro.as_str().len() as u32) + BytePos(1); // add 1 for the `!`` and pushing the macro-name portion. `visible_macro` was computed lazily from `expn_span.ctxt().outer_expn_data().kind` plus `parent_callsite` checks.
pitfalls: Removing duplicate macro spans before sorting by dominator order can retain a span that does not dominate the others, changing which macro mapping survives.
Appending split `SpanFromMir` values at the end invalidates the earlier sort; the final span sort must still run.
Only bang macros (`MacroKind::Bang`) are treated as visible macros; other expansion kinds must map to `None`.
Do not split closure spans even when they carry a visible macro.
An invalid macro-name split point must not panic or produce malformed mappings; retain the original span in release builds, as the old code explicitly guarded against `#117788`.
Async functions intentionally ignore body spans because the desugared outer function would produce unhelpful spans; only the signature span is kept.
The empty-body signature-span discard is behavior-preserving but explicitly marked with a FIXME, so it should not be generalized as a semantic invariant.
Old and new coverage mappings are only *almost* identical; expecting byte-identical `.cov-map` output across the hoist is incorrect.
preconditions: Spans are extracted per BCB statement/terminator and unexpanded back into the function `body_span`.
`is_async_fn` keeps only the function-signature span and ignores all spans from the desugared MIR body.
If no body spans were extracted, the signature span is discarded by checking `initial_spans.len() == 1` and clearing it.
Before unwanted macro spans are removed, spans must be sorted with `basic_coverage_blocks.cmp_in_dominator_order` so the retained first same-span macro span is likely to dominate the others.
`split_visible_macro_spans` runs after duplicate-macro removal and before the final span sort; split spans are appended, so prior sorting is not preserved.
The split point is the macro-name length plus one for `!`; if the split point is invalid, the original span must be retained rather than panicking or emitting malformed mappings.
Closures are exempt from macro-span deduplication and splitting (`covspan.is_closure` is retained unchanged).
`visible_macro` is derived from the expansion ancestor just before the unexpanded body span, and only `ExpnKind::Macro(MacroKind::Bang, name)` counts as a visible macro.
analysis.summary: InstrumentCoverage hoists two macro-span special cases out of the main span-refinement loop into from-MIR preprocessing: duplicate branch-macro span removal and visible-macro invocation splitting. This is a code-structure/behavior-refactor optimization, not a confirmed bug fix. Correct hoisting depends on sorting extracted spans in BCB dominator order before deduplication, and re-sorting after appending split spans.
analysis.testStrategy: Use the `tests/coverage` UI-style coverage tests rather than claiming compiler execution. Construct focused Rust inputs with (1) `debug_assert!`/`assert!` inside a closure, (2) a branch-expanding macro whose MIR gives multiple same-span BBs, and (3) a visible macro invocation in the function body. Compare `.coverage` line counts and `.cov-map` mappings/expression counts against the supplied expected changes. Verify the macro name plus `!` is represented separately from the remainder, duplicate same-span macro mappings are removed, closure spans survive deduplication, and invalid macro split points fall back to the unsplit span. Include an async function and a body with no extractable spans to exercise the signature-span rules.
analysis.trigger: Coverage instrumentation of a Rust function whose MIR yields multiple extracted spans for the same branch-expanding macro invocation (e.g. `assert!`, `debug_assert!`, `trace!`, `info!`), or whose body contains a macro invocation visible from the function body. Also triggered by async functions, closures, and functions whose body yields no extractable coverage spans.
